    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Lufthansa announced Columbus’ first scheduled nonstop flight to Europe last month. Now the city council has refused to approve the first $300,000 of the mayor’s promised support for it. The Frankfurt flights are still scheduled to start May 5, 2027. But the fight exposes something that tends to get lost in the celebration of a new international route: local officials helped make the numbers work by offering up taxpayer money to protect the airline if route revenue falls short, and the city’s portion still needed council approval. Lufthansa looks to fly Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays using a Boeing 787-9 with Allegris business class. There’ll be 28 business class seats, 28 premium economy seats and 231 coach seats. The region has 38 German companies, Bayer is building a pharmaceutical plant in New Albany, and Frankfurt offers connections throughout Europe and beyond. With the city using residents’ money to guarantee it, Lufthansa’s downside is protected trying it out. The revenue guarantee draws support from several sources: Contributor Reported Support City of Columbus Up to $1 million over three years. Council blocked the proposed first $300,000 installment. Franklin County Up to $1 million over three years. JobsOhio Participating, with the amount not publicly confirmed. Councilmember Rob Dorans states his briefing identified $1 million. Columbus Partnership and local businesses Financial support promised, with the amount undisclosed. Lufthansa would collect under the guarantee if revenue falls below the agreed target, subject to caps and a three year limit. The airport’s current incentive program also offers Frankfurt service $1 million in marketing support over two years, plus two years of landing fee, terminal rent and international inspection fee waivers. That’s available as long as they operate at least 100 departures annually over at least six months. The city’s $300,000 was included in a proposed $1 million grant to One Columbus, the regional economic development organization. On November 16, council unanimously removed the airline money and subsequently approved the remaining $700,000. Dorans objects both to the spending priority and to how the deal was handled. He says residents needing help should come first, and accuses the administration of negotiating without council involvement. The administration says all nine councilmembers were offered briefings and eight participated, including Dorans. Meanwhile, Council President Shannon Hardin is running for mayor against the incumbent whose administration owns this deal. And the councilmember who introduced the amendment pulling funding actually supports the funding. That was a maneuver that allows him to bring the funding back for another vote. You’d expect Lufthansa to have an agreement spelling out its revenue guarantee before announcing the flight. Oops. It appears not every organization contributing money already made a firm commitment. The city ordinance was seeking authority to enter into a grant agreement with One Columbus. The council wasn’t technically voting to cancel a Lufthansa contract, just on whether to appropriate the funds to the entity that had promised Lufthansa a fixed guarantee. The Columbus Partnership says it still expects the flight to happen. Council could reconsider, or other backers could fill the funding gap. I’ve covered this sort of bidding for service before, including Austin offering incentives for international flights and Pittsburgh subsidizing Qatar Airways cargo service. Usually these subsidies either go to flights that would have made money anyway, or get burned through and the flight goes away. Meanwhile, I’m betting that the money comes back.     💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s.
    • To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet currently consists of 25 planes, including:.
    • Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was confirmed by the company’s CEO at this week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s. This is interesting on many levels — we’ll see the larger Dreamliners get all-new business class cabins plus premium economy for the first time, we’ll see the smaller Dreamliners get the old business class cabins of the bigger Dreamliners, and we’ll see the airline adopt some Delta-style branding.

    To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet currently consists of 25 planes, including:.

    Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was confirmed by the company’s CEO at this week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.

    Industry observers note that the proposal is for the 787-9s to get all-new cabins, and in the process, the 787-8s will get the old business class seats from the 787-9s. That means the 787-8s will get reverse herringbone seats, which are still competitive, but of course not cutting edge (though still a huge improvement over the pairs of seats at the moment on the planes).

    Recent findings suggest that the 787-9s will really become the next-generation flagship planes for the airline, though some patience will be required. The expectation is that the first of these Dreamliners will be retrofitted in the next 18 to 24 months (so hopefully by some point in 2028), and then it’ll likely take a couple of years for the fleet to be upgraded.

    According to recent reports, we’ll talk more about the new business class product as such in a bit, but the idea is that the 787-9s will get business class suites, including a front row “business class plus” product. On top of that, the 787-9s will be getting a premium economy cabin for the first time.

    The plane will also have up to 70% more premium seats than before. Currently, Aeromexico’s 787-9s have 36 business class seats, while the retrofitted planes will have a total of 61 premium seats, between business class and premium economy. So I suspect the business class cabin won’t actually get that much bigger, but instead, most of that premium addition will come in the form of the new premium economy cabin.

    It’s also worth mentioning that Aeromexico is adopting some Delta-style branding, as Delta owns a 20% stake in Aeromexico, and the two airlines have a close partnership.

    Aeromexico’s new premium products will be known as Premier One Suites Plus (the “business class plus” product), Premier One Suites (business class), and Premier (premium economy). It seems the 787-8 business class will just be branded as Premier One, given the lack of suites with doors. That all sure seems to be inspired by the Delta One branding that’s used by the carrier’s partner.

    Seth Miller from PaxEx.Aero flags how Aeromexico’s newly introduced Boeing 787-9 business class suite is from Recaro, as the airline is reportedly the launch customer for this new product. However, the exact product hasn’t actually been named.

    Aeromexico CEO Dr. Andres Conesa unveiled the carrier's newly introduced premium economy cabin plus refreshed business class seat at #APEXFTEExpo in Singapore this week.Full teaser video in the story: paxex.aero/first-look-a….#PaxEx$RTX.

    I believe this might be an evolution of the Recaro R7 product (LATAM’s newest 787 business class), which in and of itself was already an evolution of the Recaro CL6720 product (Iberia’s newest A350 business class).

    It seems that what was unveiled earlier this year was the fresh Recaro R7 Horizon concept, which is the same idea, but with upgraded technology and customization.

    I imagine that we’ll learn more in the coming months, as this was an unusual way to unveil a newly introduced product. But this does seem to be officially happening, so it’s something to look forward to… down the road.

    Aeromexico is planning some substantial upgrades to its Dreamliners. The Boeing 787-9s will be getting all-fresh cabins, including new business class suites, plus a premium economy cabin for the first time. There will even be a premium business product in the first row, with the products marketed as Premier One Suites Plus, Premier One Suites, and Premier.

    Recent findings suggest that as this happens, the 787-8s will be getting the old reverse herringbone seats from the 787-9s, so that will be a meaningful upgrade as well. You can expect these new cabins to roll out starting at some point in 2028, so some patience will be required. I can’t wait to learn more!

    #7207. Industry News: Hah: Emirates Puts Auditors On Flights To “Provide Support & Guidance” To Crew

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1296 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Hah: Emirates Puts Auditors On Flights To “Provide Support & Guidance” To Crew

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1296 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Emirates is known for its incredibly high service standards, and that’s largely thanks to the hierarchical system onboard.
    • This system ensures that there’s accountability onboard, and I think that lack of hierarchy is one of the reasons we have service challenges at airlines in the US, as no one is really in charge.
    • Industry observers note that emirates has a rank above pursers, which are the Standard Pursers (which is a weird name, but the idea is that they’re there to audit and enforce “standards”).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Emirates is known for its incredibly high service standards, and that’s largely thanks to the hierarchical system onboard. You have different ranks of flight attendants, then you have supervisors overseeing business class and economy, and then those supervisors report to the purser.

    This system ensures that there’s accountability onboard, and I think that lack of hierarchy is one of the reasons we have service challenges at airlines in the US, as no one is really in charge. Anyway, along those lines, Emirates has just introduced a latest initiative, which will no doubt be controversial among flight attendants….

    Industry observers note that emirates has a rank above pursers, which are the Standard Pursers (which is a weird name, but the idea is that they’re there to audit and enforce “standards”). These are specially trained former pursers who no longer work flights in a standard capacity (at least until now), but instead, they audit the crews onboard flights. They have completely different uniforms.

    Emirates’ Chief Operations Officer, Adel Alredha, has just taken to Instagram to highlight a new initiative involving this small group of employees:.

    On 3 November, Emirates introduced a new initiative on select flights, which will have Standard Pursers work alongside cabin crew teams to provide support and guidance to ensure consistently high standards of service.

    This step reflects the airline’s ongoing commitment to maintaining service quality and elevating the customer experience.

    So rather than just auditing the cabins, these Emirates employees will actually be working in the cabin, and that’s sure to ruffle some feathers….

    A post shared by Adel Alredha (@adelalredha).

    Emirates is of course an incredibly global airline with staff from around the world, and I know a thing or two about the internal politics that crews deal with, the different working environments based on who is purser, etc.

    For example, you have some pursers who are incredibly strict to the point that they make their colleagues feel uncomfortable and nervous, while you have other pursers who try to encourage good service by creating a fun environment, etc.

    Sources indicate that it goes without saying that historically when a flight had an auditor onboard, everyone would be on their absolute best behavior. In a way that’s no doubt a bit chaotic and stressful, since they’re worried about repercussions if something goes wrong.

    When it comes to this initiative, on the one hand, it’s probably good for these auditors to get some renewed firsthand experience with service, guest expectations, etc. On the other hand, I have to imagine that from the perspective of other crew members, this won’t necessarily be perceived as an effort to “provide support and guidance.”.

    As one commenter on the Instagram post notes, “this is like sending a child to school along with mama with a stick to correct the kid every step.” Another commenter notes “as if there wasn’t already enough pressure on the crew.”.

    In a recent development, I am curious if these flights are still staffed with a regular purser in addition to this special rank of purser, because that could also cause a bit of a butting-of-heads. If an auditor is onboard in their official capacity, it’s clear what everyone’s role onboard is (everyone is there to make sure they perform well!). But if the auditor is there to simply “provide support,” that blurs the lines a little bit, no?

    Anyway, there aren’t actually that many of these auditor pursers at the airline, so presumably only a small percentage of flights will have them. But if you do notice a crew member with a completely different uniform (more silver in color), now you know what’s going on. That would also be a great person to provide any feedback to, because they actually have the ability to get those details to the right person.

    Emirates has Standard Pursers, who are essentially auditors who are assigned select flights, in order to evaluate service from the crew. As of this month, these auditors are also starting to work on flights alongside the crew, to “provide support and guidance.”.

    There’s no denying that this is an initiative that will make some crew members nervous, since this definitely blurs the line of auditing vs. having an extra set of helping hands. However, given the relatively small number of auditors, they shouldn’t be on too many flights. But if you do see someone in a completely different uniform (other than the standard female purser uniform), then now you know what’s going on.

    What do you make of this Emirates initiative?

    Industry News: Rove rolls out personalized shopping offers with up to 25 miles per dollar

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thepointsguy

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Rove has grown quickly since launching in 2025, expanding to 22 airline and hotel transfer partners.
    • Online shopping portals and card-linked merchant offers are some of the best ways to earn additional rewards on top of what you earn from your credit card.
    • Here's what you should know about Rove's upcoming offerings.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rove has grown quickly since launching in 2025, expanding to 22 airline and hotel transfer partners. Now, just in time for the holiday shopping season, Rove has launched personalized shopping offers that let members earn up to 25 Rove miles per dollar on select purchases. The program has also expanded its in-store shopping offers.

    Online shopping portals and card-linked merchant offers are some of the best ways to earn additional rewards on top of what you earn from your credit card. TPG's November 2026 valuations peg Rove miles at 2.05 cents apiece, so earning 25 Rove miles per dollar could yield rewards of up to 51.25 cents per dollar spent.

    Here's what you should know about Rove's upcoming offerings.

    Rove members already know they can navigate to the shopping tab on the Rove website or app and see featured offers or search for a specific merchant.

    Now, Rove members who link and connect an eligible payment card can access personalized offers in the For You section of Rove's website and app.

    Industry observers note that when a personalized offer has a higher earning rate than Rove's standard offer, you'll see both rates displayed. Since these offers are personalized, the available merchants and earning rates may vary by member.

    You'll need to activate each offer before making a qualifying purchase. Click the plus button to activate, and then check the circle that replaces the plus after activation to see how long you have to use the offer.

    Be sure to review each offer's terms before purchasing, including where the offer is valid, when it expires and whether any spending limits or purchase exclusions apply.

    By reviewing the Hyatt House and Hyatt Studios offer I enrolled in, I found it is only valid for stays within the U.S. This is too bad, as I was excited to use it for an upcoming Hyatt House stay in Canada until I read its terms.

    According to recent reports, finally, it's worth noting that neither TPG's Lyndsey Matthews nor I saw any offers in our For You sections for 25 miles per dollar spent. Instead, 15 miles per dollar spent on a new Sam's Club membership purchase is the best offer either of us found in our accounts.

    Related: Why the holiday season is the best time to start earning points and miles.

    Rove initially introduced in-store card-linked offers in August. It now claims members can earn miles on qualifying purchases at hundreds of participating physical retailers.

    According to recent reports, to earn Rove miles on an in-store purchase, link an eligible card to Rove and review the merchant's offer before making a purchase. Activate the offer first if required, then use your linked card to make a qualifying purchase. Rove says transactions are automatically tracked after the charge clears and that miles typically post within seven days.

    Related: 5 tips to maximize rewards and avoid debt this holiday shopping season.

    Rove's personalized offers could be a lucrative way to earn transferable rewards on purchases you already planned to make, especially when targeted rates reach 25 miles per dollar.

    However, offers and earning rates will vary by member, so check the For You section and review the activation and purchase requirements before shopping. You should also compare Rove's rate with other shopping portals and check for card-linked merchant offers you may be able to stack with your purchase.

    A Top Frequent Flyer Complained About American Airlines Selling Their Free Upgrade For $91—Gets Told To Delete Their Post

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3098 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that an American Airlines Executive Platinum status member took to twitter to complain that a flight they were taking the next day still had seats available, and American was offering first class to any passenger in coach for just $91, while ignoring their upgrade benefits.
    • The AAdvantage program offers upgrades to those with Executive Platinum status starting 100 hours prior to departure (not 72 as this member mentions) but that is out of seats that the airline decides to make available at no charge.
    • But what’s drawing reaction is American’s response, “Please delete this from public view.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that an American Airlines Executive Platinum status member took to twitter to complain that a flight they were taking the next day still had seats available, and American was offering first class to any passenger in coach for just $91, while ignoring their upgrade benefits. The AAdvantage program offers upgrades to those with Executive Platinum status starting 100 hours prior to departure (not 72 as this member mentions) but that is out of seats that the airline decides to make available at no charge. Here they’re looking for some amount of money from anyone – $91 from a once a year flyer rather than offering a complimentary upgrade to someone who may be generating $20,000 – $50,000 a year in ticket sales or the equivalent value in partner transactions like cobrand credit card spending. But what’s drawing reaction is American’s response, “Please delete this from public view.” We can understand why this feels frustrating. Your loyalty is genuinely appreciated, and we’re sorry this experience left you feeling overlooked. Please delete this from public view and join us in DM.

    The AAdvantage program offers upgrades to those with Executive Platinum status starting 100 hours prior to departure (not 72 as this member mentions) but that is out of seats that the airline decides to make available at no charge. Here they’re looking for some amount of money from anyone – $91 from a once a year flyer rather than offering a complimentary upgrade to someone who may be generating $20,000 – $50,000 a year in ticket sales or the equivalent value in partner transactions like cobrand credit card spending.

    But what’s drawing reaction is American’s response, “Please delete this from public view.”.

    We can understand why this feels frustrating. Your loyalty is genuinely appreciated, and we’re sorry this experience left you feeling overlooked. Please delete this from public view and join us in DM.

    @rawdbee We can understand why this feels frustrating. Your loyalty is genuinely appreciated, and we’re sorry this experience left you feeling overlooked. Please delete this from public view and join us in DM.

    — americanair (@AmericanAir) November 18, 2026.

    The important takeaway here is that upgrades are mostly dead, that this is generally true across major U.S. carriers, but hiding this isn’t the reason American Airlines asks this customer to delete their tweet.

    If this passenger is shocked by $91 upgrade offers, wait till they learn about American Airlines selling upgrades to infrequent customers for $40 (or Delta Delta doing it for $26) rather than honoring the promised complimentary benefit. And wait until they learn that pilots have priority over them too while deadheading.

    Sources indicate that of course American Airlines “genuinely appreciate[s]” a customer’s loyalty when they’re being given business by someone based on the promise of an upgrade benefit that they don’t actually need to deliver, selling their excess seats for tens of dollars rather than providing those seats the way they traditionally did as a perk for someone that’s provided tens of thousands of dollars of business. They appreciate the customer sticking around even when they’re no longer delivering the perks.

    Lest you think this is uniquely an American Airlines issue, not only have I seen Delta upsell seats for even less than American (on both domestic and long haul international routes), but United Airlines was equally a pioneer of the technique – they used to pitch infrequent flyers not just on the upgrade itself but that a paid upgrade would leapfrog them over a loyal customer.

    According to recent reports, I imagine – though American failed to explain this – the reason they’d suggest removing the tweet is because the image of the passenger’s reservation includes the reservation number. A bad actor who sees it might use it to social engineer access to the booking and make changes. It’s not advisable to publicly post a “PNR” (passenger name record) on the internet even if probably nobody does anything with it. Airlines generally tell customers their status upgrades are no longer available on the cheapest (basic economy) fares. Frontier Airlines is introducing first class, but saying even their top Diamond members will only be eligible for complimentary upgrades if they spend extra by buying a bundle. Elites are asked to purchase a lottery ticket on top of their regular ticket for the change of an upgrade, in a game that’s rigged because the airline determines whether there’s a prize at all (narrator: there usually isn’t). My issue isn’t the airline’s right to make this decision that they value $40 from a one a year flyer over rewarding the loyalty of a $30,000 a year customer, or someone spending $200,000 or more on an airline’s credit card (though this may be unwise). Instead, it’s the disconnect between the airline’s marketing and what they now actually deliver. Airlines promise upgrades as a benefit of customer loyalty. For many decades they delivered this. Now they not only fail to deliver it the way they did in the past, that failure is intentional, traded for minor ducats from low value flyers. Earlier this year, American Airlines CEO Robert Isom spoke to investors and explained the strategy selling buy ups instead of giving out free upgrades in the same merchandising category as “pre-purchase bags, checked baggage.” Twenty years ago 90% of first class seats went to upgrades and awards. Ten years ago it was about half. Now only around 12% of seats are left for Delta SkyMiles elite members. And that means on many routes and flights there are no upgrades at all. The real effect of this is to make top status unappealing. It removes upgrades as the argument for status, and that used to be the main motivator. It’s mid-tier status that’s now the sweet spot: priority check-in (shorter lines with bags) priority boarding (overhead bin space) free checked bags extra legroom coach seat The value in being at the top of the list of flyers that do not clear for an upgrade is minimal. Still, the extra value in top status is not zero. I value being able to add an extra segment to an American Airlines itinerary as a backup when my flights are delayed, without having to make the decision to switch flights right away. For many flyers that’s pretty niche. For most it’s not worth chasing. Delta works to convince flyers that extra legroom economy seats are an upgrade (“The biggest trick the devil in Atlanta ever played was convincing flyers he doesn’t exist”). They even run an upgrade process to get into those seats. But that just reinforces the notion that status which is sufficient to get into these extra legroom seats is all you need to work to attain. The problem for airlines isn’t just that this reduces the incentive for their best customers to keep flying with them. It’s that elite members are the ones most likely to get and spend on their credit cards. And they’ve been leaning into status as the biggest reason for these customers to focus their spending this way. What I’d like to see is airlines return to offering meaningful benefits even in the face of monetizing unsold first class seats for tens of dollars to once a year customers. They could offer a discount on paid upgrades in lieu of complimentary upgrades. American Airlines will already discount their tickets, including award tickets, all day long – employees and family members can book ‘AA20’ fares for 20% off. Other airlines have similar programs. So offering upgrades at 20% off for elites could make real sense. Similarly, cobrand cardmembers at Delta and United get discounts on award redemption (at Delta this is really just charging non-cardmembers more). That model could be replicated with upgrades. They could bring back middle seat blocking on flights that aren’t full, keeping the seats next to top elite members empty until they’re actually needed at the gate. That’s easier to manage now that much of gate work is being automated. I use a $70 per hour rubric on whether it was worth paying to upgrade, though this is dependent on whether I think I’ll get the upgrade free, anyway (and the cheaper the upgrade, the more likely the airline thinks they won’t sell the seat) and what seat I already have (an exit row aisle makes me less likely to pay than a middle seat in back of regular coach). The truth is though that on a flight up to 1,500 miles I’m perfectly happy with an exit row aisle, secured with status. And I’ve been.. fine? First class gets me a bit of extra seat width, but the meal isn’t worth the buy up and I’m generally not day drinking on domestic flights. I plug in and focus on work for the full flight and barely notice my surroundings.     📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (938 w)
    📖 Baca

    Industry News: Bilt Rent Day Promotion December 2026: JetBlue Mosaic Status Challenge

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Bilt is the platform known for providing rewards for housing payments.
    • Sources indicate that there are many innovative things about Bilt, including that there’s a Bilt Rent Day promotion on the first day of each month.
    • There are a couple of aspects to the Bilt Rent Day promotion, including the ability to earn bonus points (which is the same every month), plus at least one additional promotion.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Bilt is the platform known for providing rewards for housing payments. Earlier this year we saw massive changes at Bilt, including an overhaul of the credit card portfolio, plus upcoming ways that housing rewards are offered.

    Sources indicate that there are many innovative things about Bilt, including that there’s a Bilt Rent Day promotion on the first day of each month. With a fresh month being right around the corner, I’d like to cover the details of the December 2026 Bilt Rent Day offer, as it includes both a JetBlue Mosaic elite status challenge, as well as an up to 100% bonus on statement credit redemptions (which isn’t a very good deal). It’s interesting to see a second month in a row with no transfer bonus….

    There are a couple of aspects to the Bilt Rent Day promotion, including the ability to earn bonus points (which is the same every month), plus at least one additional promotion.

    Note that Bilt Rent Day promotions are generally valid from 12:00AM ET until 11:59PM PT, so technically you have around 27 hours to take advantage of them.

    Bilt has a portfolio of credit cards, including the no annual fee Bilt Blue Card (learn more), $95 annual fee Bilt Obsidian Card (learn more), and $495 annual fee Bilt Palladium Card (learn more) (Rates & Fees). Personally, I think the Bilt Palladium Card is by far the most lucrative.

    Sources indicate that on the first day of each month, you earn double those rewards on these cards, and earn up to 1,000 bonus points each month. It could be worth strategically making some purchases on the first day of each month to maximize this as much as possible.

    For example, with double points, the Bilt Palladium Card offers 4x points on everyday spending on the first day of the month, so that’s pretty awesome (up to a cap of $500 worth of spending, since that would earn you 1,000 bonus points).

    According to recent reports, on December 1, 2026, Bilt is offering a bonus when members redeem points for statement credits. The bonus you’re eligible for depends on which Bilt credit card you have, as follows:.

    Let me cut to the chase — don’t redeem your points this way. It’s a bad value. Ordinarily you get 0.55 cents per Bilt point for statement credit redemptions, so even with a 100% bonus, you’re looking at getting 1.1 cents per point. Hard pass.

    On December 1, 2026, Bilt is offering a JetBlue TrueBlue Mosaic status match challenge, and the status you’re eligible for depends on your Bilt elite status, as follows:.

    According to recent reports, the status is matched for a period of three months, with no additional activity required to maintain it for that period. Then during that three months, members can extend the status through January 31, 2028, by completing the following requirements:.

    It has been revealed that regardless of which tier you initially match to, the status you get to keep is based on the activity over the course of those three months. As a reminder, you earn one tile for every $1,000 spent on JetBlue, or every $10,000 spent on a co-branded JetBlue credit card. So renewing status requires anywhere from $1,000 to $4,000 of airfare spending, or $10,000 to $40,000 of credit card spending.

    This of course comes at a generally useful time for JetBlue elite status, given that the airline is introducing first class, with space available upgrades being an elite perk. However, it’s worth emphasizing that this really isn’t such a special offer, as it’s basically just JetBlue’s standard status match challenge offer. Except in this case, you can unlock it with Bilt elite status rather than airline elite status.

    On the first day of each month, Bilt offers a Rent Day promotion. In addition to earning up to double points for purchases, for December 2026, there are two offers members can take advantage of.

    One offer is for up to a 100% bonus on statement credit redemptions, which can get you at most 1.1 cents per point of value. Please don’t redeem your points that way. JetBlue is also offering a status match challenge, whereby Bilt members can receive Mosaic 1 or Mosaic 2 status for a period of 90 days, and can then extend status through early 2028, with the opportunity to earn up to Mosaic 3 status, based on how many tiles are earned.

    Are you taking advantage of the Bilt Rent Day promotion for December 2026?

    Membership is free and takes no more information than commenting as a guest. Earn status points for good contributions, and see fewer ads as your status grows.

    Your feedback is important in helping us keep our community safe.

    The comments on this page have not been provided, reviewed, approved or otherwise endorsed by any advertiser, and it is not an advertiser's responsibility to ensure posts and/or questions are answered.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Progressive advocates call on House Democrats to force Cuba vote

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (870 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May.
    • Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the matter is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.
    • Industry observers note that “The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the matter is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

    Industry observers note that “The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

    Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

    At problem is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”.

    The letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

    Recent findings suggest that advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly said it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the issue.

    Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they plan to bring up a vote next year.

    According to recent reports, senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

    Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

    The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

    “I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

    “Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump stated, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

    Recent findings suggest that trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

    While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

    “Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most important stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations said. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”.

    In a recent development, the House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

    The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the concern.

    In a recent development, “Across the political spectrum,” the letter said, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to newly introduced national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, loyalty Lobby flagged Accor’s pre-Black Friday subscription sale.
    • Industry observers note that accor is much bigger than its presence in the United States would have you think.
    • Industry observers note that their brands include Fairmont, Raffles, Sofitel and MGallery at the luxury end, along with Swissôtel, Pullman and Mövenpick.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, loyalty Lobby flagged Accor’s pre-Black Friday subscription sale. Combined with a weakened Brazilian currency this creates an opportunity.

    Industry observers note that accor is much bigger than its presence in the United States would have you think. The French hotel tech giant finished September with 5,857 hotels and 885,219 rooms. They operate in more than 110 countries, with a huge presence in Europe and extensive coverage in Asia and Australia.

    Industry observers note that their brands include Fairmont, Raffles, Sofitel and MGallery at the luxury end, along with Swissôtel, Pullman and Mövenpick. Then there are Novotel and Mercure, and the budget ibis brands. U.S. options include Fairmont Austin and Raffles Boston.

    I took advantage of the Bilt status match I wrote about this summer, which offered up to Platinum.

    According to recent reports, accor points are worth 2 euro cents apiece toward eligible hotel stays. The familiar redemption is 2,000 points for €40. Using November 18 exchange rates, that’s about $43.87, or 2.19 U.S. cents per point.

    Industry observers note that there’s no hotel award chart. An expensive room requires more points. But you can apply points to paid rates without hunting for a limited supply of standard award rooms, and a lower room rate means fewer points needed also.

    Reward points normally expire after 12 months without eligible earning activity. A qualifying points credit extends the whole balance, even if you earn just one point. Partner earning can keep the account alive without another hotel stay. An active ALL Signature subscription also protects Reward points from expiration.

    Industry observers note that here’s the calculation using the published monthly prices multiplied by 12, less 20%, and November 18 exchange rates. Dollar amounts are rounded.

    Your card’s conversion rate will also differ slightly, and be sure to use a card without foreign transaction fees.

    Industry observers note that the Explorer blueprint is the better pure points purchase. You’re buying hotel credit for about 29.8% below its redemption value, compared with 23.8% for Absolute. Absolute buys more points and more status credit, but each redeemable point costs more.

    In a recent development, you can stack this with ALL Accor+ Explorer, a separate paid membership offering 15% off eligible rates at participating hotels worldwide, plus benefits concentrated in Asia Pacific. Accor uses “Explorer” for both a Signature subscription tier and a different membership. Apparently someone thought that was a good idea.

    In a recent development, buying discounted points and then spending them against an eligible discounted room rate is where this gets better. Combining a 15% room discount with points purchased 29.8% below face value produces about 40.3% off the underlying room price, before the separate membership cost and the rewards you’d otherwise earn.

    There are limits to that stack:.

    Sources indicate that signature’s monthly Status points are separate from its redeemable Reward points. Absolute supplies 1,000 Status points a month, or 12,000 over a full year, versus the 14,000 needed for Platinum. Those points count in the calendar year they’re credited and reset at year end.

    There’s also an escape valve if your hotel intends change: Accor points transfer to airlines.

    According to recent reports, many other partners offer a worse ratio. British Airways, for instance, takes 4,000 Accor points for just 2,000 Avios. Use Iberia for Avios rather than accepting half as many through British Airways.

    At the Explorer subscription price above, you’re acquiring points for about 1.54 cents each. That’s also the acquisition cost of a mile through a 1:1 transfer. But once you have the points, moving them to an airline means giving up about 2.19 cents each in hotel credit.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1335 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.
    • As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.
    • However, I swiftly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.

    As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.

    However, I swiftly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.

    Recent findings suggest that I needed to get from Buenos Aires to Mendoza for a friend’s 40th birthday celebrations. Options were pretty limited, with nonstop flights available with either JetSmart or, indeed, Aerolíneas Argentinas. I try to avoid low-cost airlines when possible, because, quite simply, I enjoy the flying experience, and low-cost airlines tend to suck every enjoyable element out of it.

    Other pros to booking Aerolíneas Argentinas, personally:.

    After researching my options, I used Flying Blue miles to book two single tickets from Buenos Aires Jorge Newbery Aeroparque Airport (AEP) to Mendoza’s El Plumerillo Airport (MDZ).

    I can’t remember how much the fares were when I was planning the trip, but each one-way flight cost a total of 7,500 miles and less than $10 in taxes and fees.

    Looking now at example fares for January next year, round-trips for Aerolíneas’ lowest and most restrictive fare category (more on that to come) start at around $120.

    It has been revealed that I know it’s not a hard-and-fast rule, but I’ve come to expect that, most of the time, the baggage allowance listed on the booking confirmation is correct. This is often true with redemptions, such as British Airways, which notably offers and acknowledges a 23 kg baggage allowance when redeeming Avios, even for a short-haul flight in economy.

    The confirmation email I received clearly noted 1x checked bag with a 23 kg limit.

    Again, the attached PDF stated that I’d have 1x checked bag included.

    As the Argentinian scamsters would have it, I learned at check-in that the airline has a 15 kg weight limit for checked bags on domestic flights. I tried to plead my case and showed the rather unhelpful check-in agent my booking confirmation, but he basically said, “that means nothing.”.

    Industry observers note that so they weigh your bag, give you a ticket, and then you have to exit the terminal building and find this little cashier where they collect their scammy little earnings. And what better place to proudly display a “SkyTeam Alliance Member” sign at the very desk where the airline also proudly collects baggage fees from SkyTeam elite status holders, even when traveling on award tickets?

    Recent findings suggest that once I’d been charged the fee of around $17, I had to join another queue back inside and show them I’d paid for the extra weight before they’d dispatch my bag. You might look at the $32 in fees I paid and think, “What is he complaining about?” But this isn’t about the actual amount of money; it’s the principle.

    Only after the debacle did I learn the extent of Aerolíneas Argentinas’ domestic fare restrictions. Imagine paying $510 (more than four times the cheapest fare) for a “premium economy” ticket and still only getting 15 kg checked baggage allowance, no Fast Pass, no priority boarding (what?), and no lounge access. The latter isn’t such a significant deal as Aerolíneas Argentinas doesn’t even have its own lounge at AEP. The real kicker is that Aerolíneas restricts SkyTeam’s Sky Priority benefits to its two most expensive fares.

    Airline loyalty is really vital to me, and I generally value it more than the ability to redeem miles. Maybe I’ll get into that another day….

    Things got off to a fairly normal start when I saw the Sky Priority check-in kiosks at Aeroparque.

    That feeling of normalcy lasted as long as it took me to get from the sign to the aforementioned conversation about the checked bag situation at the desk. Despite my very best efforts combining my Castilian Spanish and Geordie charm (we’re called Geordies where I’m from in the North East of England), the man at the check-in desk seemed to take real pleasure in explaining that the checked bag rules on my booking confirmation were irrelevant and I’d have to pay the fee.

    For what it’s worth, Sky Priority check-in was also available at Mendoza.

    Being nickel-and-dimed for a checked bag by a flag carrier airline is shameful.

    Back at Aeroparque, there was no fast track, and the security line was ridiculously long. That said, it’s rare in South America to have fast track lanes. For example, no matter whether you’re flying economy or first class (even Air France La Première), everyone waits in the same line to clear pre-departure passport control at São Paulo’s Guarulhos.

    Thanks to my Priority Pass, I did have access to the surprisingly nice AMAE lounge in the national departures part of the airport.

    In a recent development, even from the outside, my 15-year-old Embraer 190 looked like it had seen better days. The zebra-striped dirt streaks running from each window suggested this place hadn’t been washed or hit the maintenance hangar for a while.

    Sources indicate that inside the Embraer, however, could have been a lot worse. The older seats had thick padding, and despite being a small 2-2-configured cabin, it felt bright and spacious.

    It was the Uber advertising on every single headrest that I found most jarring.

    The legroom was decent, too. The retro seatback screens, on the other hand, were pretty much redundant.

    In a recent development, it was stepping on board the 16-year-old Boeing 737-700 back to Buenos Aires that Aerolíneas Argentinas’ low-costness was most glaring. Looking at this, I would never guess this place belonged to a flag carrier. The seats were very uncomfortable, and I think I remember they didn’t recline either.

    As for service, I don’t recall it being particularly good or particularly bad. Forgettable is probably the most accurate word.

    Industry observers note that imagine the likes of Spirit (RIP) or Ryanair calling itself a national flag carrier; that’s basically what Aerolíneas Argentinas is. I’m planning a trip with my dad and brother for February next year that includes Argentina, and I will actively avoid flying Aerolíneas, even if it means forgoing the chance to earn any Flying Blue miles and XPs.

    It has been revealed that it’s almost as if the airline has been abandoned. After all, the only real competition is low-cost airlines at LATAM — the full-service carrier which dominates South America. Who knows, maybe things will change come 2028 when it takes delivery of fresh Airbus A330-900s and Boeing 737 MAXs.

    In a recent development, if I were a power that be at SkyTeam, I’d definitely remove the airline from the alliance. And if I had my way, Aerolíneas Argentinas would be bought by LATAM, and the cherry on top would be LATAM joining SkyTeam. I should probably put a business case together for that….

    FAA Ground Stop Blamed On Elon Musk—Here’s Why That’s Ridiculous

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 45 min read (9015 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~45 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop followed a contractor’s router installation in Arkansas.
    • Recent findings suggest that there’s a real oversight question here.
    • The November 13 nationwide departure stop began at 3:54 p.m.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop followed a contractor’s router installation in Arkansas. Now the story is becoming about Elon Musk: a claim that DOGE cut FAA employees, oversight was loosened, and this led to the flight stoppage. There’s a real oversight question here. It long predates DOGE. In fact it goes back decades. And even there, the connection between specific oversight failures and what actually happened hasn’t been made. Anyone writing about this needs to at least know that an L3Harris contractor’s router configuration error caused a nationwide air traffic disruption in 2009, too. And federal investigators criticized the FAA’s oversight after that incident! FAA problems did not begin with DOGE. A Router Change Disrupted The National Network The November 13 nationwide departure stop began at 3:54 p.m. Eastern and lasted until 8:15 p.m. Aircraft already airborne continued landing. The FAA’s preliminary account describes excessive connection attempts flooding its telecommunications network. Instability affected 17 of 22 enroute centers and spread to approach facilities. L3Harris had installed a router at a radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas. Investigators also identified a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. Blocking those sites stabilized the network, and officials disabled the relevant function on more than 60 similar routers. FAA Oversight Has Been A Problem, Long Before DOGE One Mile at a Time links the failure to DOGE, drawing on CNN’s reporting about a March 2025 maintenance memo. According to CNN, contractor maintenance shifted from requests requiring approval to notifications that could proceed without explicit approval. Liaisons were still supposed to evaluate the work, but there was a small staff handling thousands of notices. Bedford said the contractor was monitored and a risk assessment occurred. The technicians’ union says the FAA employee merely provided access. An FAA spokesperson later admitted that the escort doesn’t remain during work on L3 equipment. (To be sure, the union saying none of its members performing a risk assessment doesn’t mean nobody performed one.) Additional FAA review might have caught a problem the contractor missed. It’s speculative to suggest that FAA supervision, rathe rthan contractor supervision would have made a difference. And CNN itself describes a chronic technician shortage stretching back years – that I’ve written about several times – as a reason for the policy change. One Mile at a Time though says Elon Musk’s DOGE laid off hundreds of FAA employees, making for the biggest single year layoffs at the organization in history.In fact, the FAA fired 11,400 controllers in 1981. Here there’s no identified fired employee or eliminated review position connected to this installation. Moreover, the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union announced that its 132 fired probationary employees were being reinstated with back pay, with a March 20, 2025 return date. There were other departures. And it’s plausible DOGE was counterproductive here. I disagreed with the effort overall and didn’t expect success. But there’s just not been anything more than insinuation that that effort was related to Friday’s ground stop. A Harris Router Caused A Nationwide Disruption In 2009 On November 19, 2009, a Harris technician’s router configuration error disrupted the FAA telecommunications network during a transition to fiber. The Transportation Department’s inspector general found that roughly 75% of network routes were blocked. Restoration took five hours. Monitoring failed, and technicians struggled to locate the source. It also found that FAA oversight should have been more effective. Investigators had already called for better equipment configuration controls in 2008. The 2009 outage primarily affected flight planning and data services. But contractor router work, a problem spreading through the network, slow fault detection, and inadequate FAA oversight were documented together in a federal report sixteen years ago with this network and this contractor. The FAA struggled long before the current administration. And maintenance problems go back even further: Government auditors documented a 1997–2000 Alaska experiment that lengthened maintenance intervals and relied heavily on running equipment until failure. A July 2024 aviation industry coalition letter traced a shift toward fixing equipment after it failed to the 2013 budget sequester. As I covered in March, Bob Poole’s reporting describes decades of technician cuts. His sources put the decline at more than 6,600 technicians to roughly 4,000. Insufficient staffing and poor implementation make fixing things after they fail the general path FAA appears to have taken. I Was Skeptical Of DOGE Before Any Of This Happened Musk himself warned about this exact network on February 27, 2025. He claimed an FAA assessment put it “single digit months to catastrophic failure.” He initially blamed Verizon, then corrected himself the same day (the deteriorating system was L3Harris’s). . Elon Musk’s February 27, 2025 correction identifying L3Harris’s legacy network It’s hard to blame Musk when he was literally warning about failure of this specific network. And it demonstrates the FAA was aware of risk that predated the current administration. Indeed, DOGE was aware of the risk, and its titular head shouted it from the rooftops. I was skeptical that DOGE would fix the FAA when Duffy first invited Musk’s team in. It was asking for a cat, provided it barked. Government agencies behave as they do because of their incentives. Their problems aren’t generally that nobody smart enough or sufficiently determined has shown up to fix them. Cutting employees without changing procurement, funding, and accountability can leave the same dysfunctional institution with less ability to do its work. Singapore is an unusual example of building substantial state capacity, something of an outlier. Lee Kuan Yew deliberately recruited top talent into a prestigious public service, promoted on merit, strengthened corruption enforcement, and later added high pay. Its competence was built through institutions, rewards, and consequences. We get the government that we have for public choice reasons, and because of median voters. Three are companies that benefit from the way the system works, employees themselves, and both groups have much greater incentive to pay attention to the details than the average citizen. The programs we have, that many even deem wasteful, exist for a reason – not because of systemic incompetence. Someone benefits! The FAA Has Spent Decades Failing To Deliver Promised Upgrades The FAA was testing replacements for paper flight strips in 1983. It’s still rolling them out. Canada completed its commercial airport and terminal facility rollout by 2006, according to the Eno Transportation Center’s history of the two countries’ efforts. The inspector general’s review of NextGen shows more than $15 billion spent through 2024 and relatively little to show for it. And this administration is repeating familiar mistakes. In September, the Government Accountability Office found 11,389 separate project schedules for the latest modernization efforts, including installations at the same sites without coordinating them to minimize operational disruption. The FAA operates air traffic control and regulates its safety. Different offices handle those jobs, but they remain inside the same agency. The International Civil Aviation Organization guidance calls for independent oversight and separation of responsibilities. The FAA’s 2023 independent safety review found lack of that separation, noting that the oversight office needed the operating organization’s concurrence to gather information. The regulated operation could impede the regulator inside the same agency. I’ve laid out the Canadian alternative. NAV CANADA is a separate nonprofit with stakeholder governance and no equity shareholders. It charges users and finances investment with debt instead of waiting for Congress to fund each year’s portion of a long term project. Transport Canada regulates it. The Response To Failure Is Another Request For Billions One Mile at a Time is right to say “There obviously won’t be any accountability with this situation.” But this has been a problem across administrations. An organization that repeatedly misses its technology goals gets to use the resulting obsolescence as an argument for even more money. As I wrote this week, most of the $30.1 billion Modern Skies Act doesn’t even go to air traffic control (a majority goes to airports, primarily St. Louis – in the home state of the bill’s Senate sponsor). Now the administration wants $50 billion. Proposal Air Traffic Systems And Facilities Airport Projects $30.1 billion Modern Skies Act $12.1 billion $18 billion $50.1 billion administration request $30.1 billion $20 billion The new $50.1 billion request includes new control centers and towers as well as technology, but still bundles $20 billion in airport infrastructure and terminal spending into the response to a communications failure. Congress already supplied $12.5 billion last year. More investment may be needed. Users, not taxpayers, should be funding this. And real reforms are needed before handing the FAA tens of billions after their failed management processes squander the last tens of billions.     Recent findings suggest that there’s a real oversight question here. It long predates DOGE. In fact it goes back decades. And even there, the connection between specific oversight failures and what actually happened hasn’t been made. Anyone writing about this needs to at least know that an L3Harris contractor’s router configuration error caused a nationwide air traffic disruption in 2009, too. And federal investigators criticized the FAA’s oversight after that incident! FAA problems did not begin with DOGE.

    The November 13 nationwide departure stop began at 3:54 p.m. Eastern and lasted until 8:15 p.m. Aircraft already airborne continued landing. The FAA’s preliminary account describes excessive connection attempts flooding its telecommunications network. Instability affected 17 of 22 enroute centers and spread to approach facilities. L3Harris had installed a router at a radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas. Investigators also identified a radar site in Amarillo, Texas. Blocking those sites stabilized the network, and officials disabled the relevant function on more than 60 similar routers. FAA Oversight Has Been A Problem, Long Before DOGE One Mile at a Time links the failure to DOGE, drawing on CNN’s reporting about a March 2025 maintenance memo. According to CNN, contractor maintenance shifted from requests requiring approval to notifications that could proceed without explicit approval. Liaisons were still supposed to evaluate the work, but there was a small staff handling thousands of notices. Bedford remarked the contractor was monitored and a risk assessment occurred. The technicians’ union says the FAA employee merely provided access. An FAA spokesperson later admitted that the escort doesn’t remain during work on L3 equipment. (To be sure, the union saying none of its members performing a risk assessment doesn’t mean nobody performed one.) Additional FAA review might have caught a problem the contractor missed.     #7196. Tempers flare as future of Social Security debated

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (690 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Tempers flare as future of Social Security debated

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ron Johnson, R-Wis., stated he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).
    • If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday showed how poisonous the politics could become.
    • Budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., stated he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday showed how poisonous the politics could become.

    Budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day. Democrats erupted, accusing Johnson of scaring seniors and being unwilling to fix a financial lifeline for more than 72 million retirees.

    Recent findings suggest that “I think it’s outrageous,” stated Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., one of several Democrats on the panel who slammed Johnson for his comments. “Don’t go out there scaring Americans to make political points on Fox News. This is too fricking important.”.

    Johnson acknowledged making an “imprecise comment” on prospects for a fix during the Fox interview. But he also told Democrats that if they had read his “chairman’s memo” he sent them Tuesday they would know he wants to preserve the system and pass a law to prevent any cuts to benefits if the Social Security Trust Fund is depleted.

    Industry observers note that "This is a scam, it’s grotesque, and at this point there’s really no way to fix Social Security," he noted on Fox Business. "It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope you can recover some of your money.”.

    But Johnson appeared to contradict himself later in the same interview, saying there is a difference with a “government-sanctioned Ponzi scheme” in that “you can force investors to keep putting money into it and that’s what we’ll probably have to do … You can fix Social Security and make it solvent.”.

    In his opening statement at the hearing, Johnson stated Congress should pass a law to prevent benefit cuts and then “roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem, our massive debt and deficits.” He said that is the only way to “ensure we have the financial wherewithal to honor promises made to seniors.”.

    In a recent development, johnson also told the panel he used the term “Ponzi scheme” in part to draw attention to the importance of addressing the problem. “If I gotta pay a political price for that, I really don’t care,” he mentioned.

    It has been revealed that there is no doubt that a fix is needed. Without any change, Social Security recipients face a 22 percent cut in benefits by the end of 2032, according to projections from the Social Security Board of Trustees. Johnson noted Congress and the president won’t cut benefits even if the trust fund is exhausted.

    And there has been no shortage of Social Security bills introduced to provide a fix, but none of them has gained momentum.

    It has been revealed that sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, drew flak from fellow Republicans after he and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., proposed lifting the cap on income subject to the Social Security payroll tax so that the tax would apply to all earned income.

    A bipartisan proposal, from Sens. Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., Bill Cassidy, R-La., Tim Kaine, D-Va., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, would have put a blueprint in motion by requiring the Social Security Advisory Board to recommend a bill that would ensure Social Security is funded for at least the next 50 years.

    Senators on both sides of the aisle mentioned they were committed to fixing Social Security. Republicans stressed the importance of economic growth to bring in more revenue to the system and cautioned that tax increases would slow growth.

    Democrats pitched shifting more revenue into the system, for example by raising the cap on the payroll tax or taxing other income.

    “I do believe if we can be focused on fixing the Social Security stability issue, that could be a stepping stone to fixing broader problems,” noted Kaine, who is anticipated to chair the Budget Committee when Democrats take over Congress next year.
